title: A cycle test in the physiology lab, with a falling pressure
objective: Calculate pulse pressure and mean arterial pressure from a blood pressure reading, and interpret a narrow pulse pressure as a sign of low stroke volume
secondaryObjectives: Explain the cardiovascular response to exercise: higher heart rate and stroke volume, and blood redirected to working muscle
Explain how the baroreceptor reflex keeps blood pressure up on standing, and how the skeletal muscle pump and venous valves return blood to the heart
Calculate cardiac output from heart rate and stroke volume, and explain how preload, contractility and afterload change stroke volume

brief.situation: Exercise physiology lab, 10:00. You are running a submaximal cycle test on a classmate, Daniel Ortiz, 24, while your instructor supervises the next station. Your lab sheet asks for heart rate, blood pressure, pulse pressure and mean arterial pressure at every stage.
handover: Protocol: 2 min warm-up at 25 W, then 3-minute stages at 50, 75, 100, 125 and 150 W. A chest strap shows his heart rate live; you take each blood pressure by hand while he pedals.
Lab rules: screen before the test, resting BP seated, stop for dizziness, pallor or a systolic fall of more than 10 mmHg as the load rises, and record HR and BP for at least 4 minutes of recovery.
Tell the instructor about anything in the screening that could change the plan.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
A blood pressure takes about a minute. Calculate and interpret each reading as you go.
Partway through you are asked to write what the numbers mean. A debrief scores what you did.

read.question: What do his pulse pressure and MAP tell you about his stroke volume as the load rises, why might that be today, and what do you do now and after you stop?

parts.label: Pulse pressure, MAP and stroke volume
parts.criteria: Calculates PP as systolic minus diastolic and MAP as diastolic plus a third of PP; reads a systolic that falls as the load rises and a PP under about 25% of systolic as a narrowing pulse pressure, a sign that stroke volume is not keeping up (normally systolic rises and PP widens with exercise); links it to less blood volume the day after donating.
parts.modelAnswer: PP is systolic minus diastolic and MAP is diastolic plus a third of PP. With exercise systolic should rise and PP widen as stroke volume goes up; his systolic is falling as the load rises and his PP is narrowing toward a quarter of systolic, so his stroke volume is not keeping up. Giving blood yesterday lowered his blood volume, so preload and stroke volume fall short.

parts.label: What to do
parts.criteria: Stops the test at the fall or the first dizziness or pallor; keeps him pedaling with no load (or lies him down, legs raised) instead of stopping dead or standing him up, because the muscle pump keeps venous return up; keeps measuring for at least 4 minutes of recovery; tells the instructor.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop now. Drop the load to zero and keep him pedaling slowly so the leg muscles keep pumping blood back to the heart; if he still feels faint, lie him down with his legs raised. Don't let him stop dead or stand. Keep taking HR and BP for at least 4 minutes, and tell the instructor.

expertPath.text: Screen him: he gave blood yesterday and skipped breakfast. Resting BP 118/76. Tell the instructor before starting; he eats something.
Warm-up, then BP every stage. Calculate PP and MAP each time: diastolic plus a third of PP.
At 75 W his systolic is lower than at 50 W and PP is narrowing: stroke volume is not keeping up. Measure again early in the 100 W stage.
Systolic more than 10 below its peak as the load rises: stop, zero load, keep him pedaling slowly. BP in recovery for at least 4 minutes; tell the instructor.

fainted.headline: He fainted
fainted.body: Find the readings where systolic stopped rising and pulse pressure narrowed, and when he first went pale. After stopping, legs that keep moving (or lying with legs raised) keep blood coming back to the heart.

stoppedSafe.headline: Read the pressure, stopped, recovered
stoppedSafe.body: You calculated PP and MAP correctly, read a falling systolic and narrowing pulse pressure as low stroke volume, stopped on it and used an unloaded cool-down. That is the expert path.

stoppedLate.headline: Recovered, by a slower or riskier route
stoppedLate.body: Check when you stopped against the first fall and the first symptoms, how you stopped, and whether the screen, the resting BP and the recovery readings were done.

time_up.headline: Out of time
time_up.body: The test needs a screen, a resting BP, readings each stage and a recovery.

scoring.modelReasoning: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic; MAP is about diastolic plus a third of the pulse pressure, because the heart spends longer in diastole. During graded exercise systolic should rise with each stage (about 10 mmHg per MET) while diastolic stays about the same, so pulse pressure widens as stroke volume rises. A systolic that falls as the load rises, with a pulse pressure narrowing toward a quarter of systolic, says stroke volume is not keeping up: here the day after a blood donation, with a smaller blood volume and less preload. Dizziness, pallor and a systolic fall of more than 10 mmHg under rising load are reasons to stop. Stop with an unloaded cool-down (or lie him down with legs raised) so the skeletal muscle pump keeps venous return up; stopping dead or standing invites a faint. Record HR and BP for at least 4 minutes of recovery and tell the instructor.

ppQ.ask: While you listen: what should happen to his systolic pressure and pulse pressure as the load rises?

choices.label: Systolic rises and pulse pressure widens
Systolic falls and pulse pressure narrows

ppQ.explain: With exercise stroke volume rises, so systolic rises and pulse pressure widens while diastolic stays about the same. A narrowing pulse pressure points to low stroke volume.

coolQ.ask: Why keep him pedaling with no load instead of stopping dead?

choices.label: The leg muscles keep pumping blood back to the heart
It clears lactate so he won't be sore

coolQ.explain: After exercise, losing the skeletal muscle pump lets venous return fall and many healthy people feel faint; moving the legs keeps blood returning to the heart.
